external_narratives.summary: National Trust page about the B-17G crash on Reigate Hill on 19 March 1945, killing nine USAAF airmen from the 384th Bombardment Group. The crew were returning from bombing an oil refinery at Plauen, Germany, when their battle-damaged aircraft entered cloud and struck trees.

external_narratives.summary: Details of the 'Wing Tips' memorial sculpture by Surrey artist Roger Day. The two oak pieces are spaced exactly 32 metres (105 feet) apart, matching the B-17 wingspan. Molten metal recovered from the crash site is embedded within the sculpture.

memorial_details:
Dedicatory wooden bench with metal plaque. Also a memorial sculpture, carved from an ancient Surrey oak tree with some metal from the crash buried in the sculpture.

The memorial sculpture, created by Surrey artist Roger Day was unveiled on the 70th anniversary of the crash.

Memorial Display (Sept 2017): Boeing B-17 Flying Fortress 43-39035 was displayed as a memorial.

Exhibition (Not specified): Display of parts from the aircraft at Reigate Manor Hotel.

Unveiling of the Memorial (70th anniversary of the crash (March 19, 2015)): The memorial sculpture was unveiled. Created by Surrey artist Roger Day from ancient Surrey oak, it includes metal recovered from the crash site and is placed to match the aircraft's wingspan.
narrative: A USAAF B-17 Flying Fortress was lost over Reigate Hill, Surrey, carrying both regular aircrew and US Air Attaché Colonel Dan Benson. Pilot Robert S Griffin, 24 years old, was in command; co-pilot Herbert S Geller, Royal Runyon, Robert Manbeck, Thomas Hickey, and Philip were also among those aboard. The cause of the crash is not recorded in available sources. All crew members were killed. The site is today marked by a memorial sculpture titled *Wing Tips*, created by Surrey artist Roger Day, honouring those who died here.
